clue.text: Awkward way to separate education, on failing

indicators.note: the road letters come between and so separate the shuffled letters of the other words
something failing has gone wrong, so the letters of education and on are put into disorder

parts.note: RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a clumsy scheme is splitting up schooling, and failing at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way' is a road, abbreviated; 'failing' gives the shuffled run UNCOOINATED, which the road splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uncoordinated moves clumsily, lacking smooth control of the limbs, which is what awkward means.

clue.text: Composure, the skill of rigid wings?

definitions.meaning: calmness under pressure, not getting in a flap
whimsically, the ability of wings that cannot beat up and down: the knack of not flapping

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is playful: 'in a flap' means agitated, so the calm person and the stiff wing share the same quality of not flapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Calmness that never gets flustered is the trait of a person who cannot be rattled; literally, rigid wings cannot flap.

clue.text: Island buried under fish bones

indicators.note: in a down clue the island letter sits below the fish, as if buried beneath it

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: An island lies sunk beneath a fish's skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: The carpi are the small wrist bones; the word is the plural of carpus.

clue.text: Where's your saddle? Scram!

definitions.meaning: the saddle you sit on is mounted on your bicycle
a curt order to go away, British slang made famous by politician Norman Tebbit

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the phrase is a brusque 'clear off!', and became famous when Norman Tebbit said his unemployed father got on his bike to look for work.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase locates a seat literally on a bicycle and is also British slang telling someone to leave at once.

clue.text: Song about an aromatic plant

indicators.note: the song wraps around the next word, so these letters go about or around it

parts.note: a ditty is a short simple song
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tune is composed in praise of a fragrant herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning', the surface sense of a song on a subject, but it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dittany is a fragrant herb of the mint family, used in perfumes and herbal remedies.

clue.text: Pincers — little ones

definitions.meaning: a tool for gripping or cutting, like pliers

explanation.definitionFit: Nippers are both gripping tools such as pliers and, in British slang, small children.

clue.text: Catch subdivision up

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is written upwards, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a part is a subdivision of a whole

explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns PART upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To trap something is to catch it, as with a snare.

clue.text: He's lasted out, as immortal

indicators.note: out signals the letters of these words are knocked out of their order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
taken as written

explanation.surface: Of a long-lived man: he survived to the end, as if he could never die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lasted out' reads as endured to the end; 'out' is the anagram signal for HESLASTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deathless never dies, the plain sense of immortal.

clue.text: No spontaneous joy, when drunk?

parts.note: recorded mirth played on television is not spontaneous; and canned is slang for drunk, so it is also the laughter of a tipsy person

explanation.walkthrough: Canned is British slang for drunk, so a second picture is merriment after drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Prerecorded laughs dubbed onto a sitcom soundtrack are mirth with no live audience behind it.

clue.text: Attack in order to get positive response

parts.note: for, as in 'go for help', means in order to get
aye or ay is yes, an assent

explanation.surface: Someone tries something just to get a yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A foray is a sudden raid or attack into enemy territory.

clue.text: Boss, the pick of the bunch?

definitions.meaning: the person in charge, an informal term
playfully, the best fruit at the top of a bunch

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for the chief person, and literally suggests the finest fruit of a hand of bananas.

clue.text: A compound as ductile lowers the ph

indicators.note: compound as a verb means mix together, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Chemistry: a pliable compound reduces a solution's pH.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compound' looks like a noun of chemistry; it is the anagram signal on AS DUCTILE.
explanation.definitionFit: To acidulate is to make slightly acid, and acidity is measured as a lower pH reading.

clue.text: Toast cut in half, proving hit

indicators.note: only the first half of the toast's letters is kept

parts.note: ...-... is an old-fashioned drinking toast

explanation.surface: A toast is cut short when someone throws a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned British drinking toast, like 'cheers'; halving it gives the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To chin someone is slang for punching them on the jaw.

clue.text: Divers adapting to protect an endangered species

indicators.note: the rearranged letters surround and so protect the next word
divers is an old word for various, so the letters of adapting are made various, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Scuba divers change their methods to shield a creature at risk of extinction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like swimmers but is an archaic word for 'various', the anagram signal, giving GIANTPDA; 'to protect' then wraps it round the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The black-and-white bear of China is a classic example of an animal at risk of extinction.

clue.text: Casanova parking love by the roadside?

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

indicators.note: by in the sense of at, so the zero for love is placed at, and within, the stopping place

parts.note: a lay-by is a British roadside stopping place for vehicles
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: A womaniser parks and makes love in a lay-by.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAY-BY is a British roadside pull-in; 'love by the roadside' means O in a lay-by.
explanation.definitionFit: Casanova, the Venetian seducer, has become a byword for a man who chases women, a rich pleasure-seeker.

clue.text: A leaderless country breaking island's sound rules?

indicators.note: the shortened word breaks into the island and sits inside it

parts.note: Cos (Kos) is a Greek island

indicators.note: leaderless means the word loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: country as an adjective means rural, rustic

explanation.surface: A headless nation smashes into an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country' looks like a nation but is an adjective meaning rural; 'leaderless' trims it to USTIC, and 'breaking' sends that into a Greek island.
explanation.definitionFit: Acoustics are the principles of how sound behaves, the science of sound, hence its rules.

clue.text: Regular money as reward, put in mail

indicators.note: the reward is placed inside the word for mail

parts.note: to mail is to send
a tip is a small reward

explanation.surface: Being paid regularly as a bonus, posted out.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed regular allowance or salary, such as paid to a cleric.

clue.text: Something restricting access — with two keys?

parts.note: B is a musical key
a locker is something you lock with, another kind of key

explanation.surface: A barrier, opened only with a pair of keys.
explanation.walkthrough: The two keys are of different sorts: B is a key in music, and a locker is anything that locks, which is what a key does.
explanation.definitionFit: A blocker is anything that obstructs or prevents entry.

clue.text: Get to have each pound in pay hike

indicators.note: these letters go inside the word for a pay hike

parts.note: a rise is a British pay increase
L is the abbreviation for the pound sterling

explanation.surface: A worker gets every pound of a wage increase.
explanation.walkthrough: A rise is the British term for a pay raise; 'in' is the container signal, and 'to have' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise something is to understand it, as in 'I get it'.

clue.text: Introduced to American, a standard game

indicators.note: the answer is introduced into, and sits inside, these words of the clue

explanation.surface: An American is taught a classic pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduced to' signals the run within AmeriCAN A STAndard.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a rummy-style card game from Uruguay, a 1950s craze.

clue.text: Change from blue to green

parts.note: blue is the colour of the Conservatives, CON for short
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone changes political colour, from Tory blue to environmentalist green.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the British Conservative party's colour; vert is the heraldic term for green.
explanation.definitionFit: To convert is to transform or alter something into another form.

clue.text: Flourishing boozer

explanation.definitionFit: Lush describes thick, thriving growth and is also slang for a drunkard.

clue.text: It's essential to watch, perhaps, sea water source

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the sea
a spring is a source of water

explanation.surface: Seawater comes from an essential source.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watch' is the timepiece, not observing.
explanation.definitionFit: The coiled driving spring powers a mechanical clock, so it is the vital part; figuratively, any chief motive.

clue.text: Bar found, when caught after batting

indicators.note: the word for caught follows the word for batting

parts.note: in cricket the side batting is said to be in
got means caught, as of a fugitive

explanation.surface: Cricket: a bar is found once a batsman is caught.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman batting is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a block of cast metal, usually shaped like a bar of gold.

clue.text: One set off to make a lot of money

explanation.walkthrough: 'One set off' is something detonated, not a traveller who started out.
explanation.definitionFit: An explosive device is detonated, and in British slang a fortune is described as costing a bomb.

clue.text: Uninspiring to save launch I find on Lyme Regis beach?

indicators.note: the dull word keeps and so saves these letters inside it

parts.note: trite means hackneyed, uninspiring
to lob is to launch in a high arc

explanation.surface: A dull thing is held back to launch a discovery on a seaside beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Lyme Regis is a Dorset seaside town on the Jurassic Coast, famous for fossils; 'find' is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Trilobites are fossil marine arthropods, a classic discovery for fossil hunters on that coast.

clue.text: Dark piece on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means heard rather than seen, signalling a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the knight is a chess piece

explanation.surface: A gloomy item broadcast on air.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess piece and the dark hours sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the time of darkness, so dark serves as a noun for it.

clue.text: Content to have citizen be influential

parts.note: a subject is a citizen of a monarchy
to matter is to be important or influential

explanation.surface: Happy to see a citizen carry weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like satisfied, but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The topic dealt with in a book or talk is its content.
